# Design a URL Shortener

> **Difficulty:** `EASY` | **Target Companies:** `Bitly • TinyURL • Twitter (t.co)` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A URL shortener is really just a distributed key-value store (short code -> long URL) with one extremely **read-heavy access pattern**, so almost every real design decision is about making that one lookup fast and that one code generation ==collision-free==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a service like Bitly: a user submits a long URL and gets back a
short one (like short.ly/aZ9k2). Visiting the short URL redirects the
visitor to the original long URL. Design the system that makes this work
at scale.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: How many URLs do we need to shorten per day, and what's the read:write ratio?
*Why it matters:* URL shorteners are read-heavy by nature, usually 100:1 or more redirects to creations. That ratio decides whether you even need a cache layer, and how aggressively.

#### Q: Do short URLs need to be unguessable/random, or is a short, possibly predictable code acceptable?
*Why it matters:* This decides between a counter-based approach (predictable, simpler, sequential) and a random-generation approach (needs collision checking, but codes can't be enumerated by an attacker).

#### Q: Do users need custom aliases (choose their own short code), and do links expire?
*Why it matters:* Custom aliases mean you must handle uniqueness conflicts at write time with a clear error, not silently. Expiry means you need a background cleanup job or TTL-based storage, not just a table that grows forever.

#### Q: Do we need click analytics (how many times a link was visited, from where)?
*Why it matters:* Analytics turns this from 'one write path, one read path' into a system with an additional high-volume event-logging pipeline that must not slow down the redirect itself.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a long URL, generate and return a unique short URL.
- Given a short URL, redirect the visitor to the original long URL with low latency.
- Support optional custom aliases chosen by the user.
- Support optional expiration dates on shortened links.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Redirects must be fast: well under 100ms, since a slow redirect is a bad experience on every single click.**
- **High availability for redirects specifically: a URL shortener being briefly unable to accept new links is tolerable, being unable to redirect existing ones is not.**
- **Short codes must be effectively unique with no user-visible collisions, even under concurrent writes.**
- **The system must scale to billions of stored URLs and tens of thousands of redirects per second at peak.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 100 million new short URLs created per day
- 100:1 read-to-write ratio (10 billion redirects per day)
- Each stored URL record is roughly 500 bytes (long URL + short code + metadata)
- Links are kept for 5 years by default

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Write QPS:** 100,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 1,160 writes/sec average; design for 5-10x that at peak, so ~10,000 writes/sec
- **Read QPS:** 100:1 ratio means ≈ 116,000 reads/sec average, well over 500,000/sec at peak, this is the number that actually drives the architecture
- **Storage over 5 years:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 * 500 bytes ≈ 91 TB total, which comfortably fits a horizontally sharded relational or key-value store, not a single machine
- **Short code space needed:** 100M/day * 365 * 5 ≈ 182 billion codes; base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) with 7 characters gives 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations, comfortably enough

*Capacity Takeaway:* This is a read-dominated system by roughly two orders of magnitude, so the entire architecture should be optimized around making redirects fast and cacheable, while writes can tolerate slightly more latency.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A client hits a load balancer, which routes to a stateless fleet of app
servers. Writes (POST /shorten) go to the app server, which generates a
short code and writes it to a sharded database, the source of truth. Reads
(GET /{shortCode}) first check a distributed cache (like Redis); on a cache
hit the redirect happens immediately, on a miss the app server reads from
the database and populates the cache before redirecting. Because reads
outnumber writes by roughly 100 to 1, the cache is doing almost all of the
real work in this system, the database mostly needs to be correct and
durable, not blazing fast on every single read.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### High-level design: redirect (read) path dominates

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    lb["Load Balancer"]:::server
    app["App Servers"]:::server
    cache["Cache (Redis)"]:::cache
    db[("Sharded DB")]:::db
    queue>"Click Events Queue"]:::queue
    client --> lb
    lb --> app
    app -->|"read (hot path)"| cache
    cache -.->|"miss -> read"| db
    app -->|"write"| db
    app -.->|"log click"| queue
```

#### A redirect request, step by step

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    classDef step fill:#1e293b,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:2px,color:#f8fafc;
    step_1["1. Client requests /{shortCode} (GET)"]:::step
    step_2["2. App server checks cache (Redis lookup)"]:::step
    step_1 --> step_2
    step_3["3. Cache hit (return long_url immediately)"]:::step
    step_2 --> step_3
    step_4["4. Cache miss -> DB read (then populate cache)"]:::step
    step_3 --> step_4
    step_5["5. 301/302 redirect (browser follows to long_url)"]:::step
    step_4 --> step_5
```

#### Short code generation, hash vs counter

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  a["New long URL submitted"] --> b{"Custom alias given?"}
  b -->|"yes"| c["Check alias uniqueness"]
  b -->|"no"| d["Generate code"]
  d --> e{"Hash or counter?"}
  e -->|"hash"| f["Base62-encode hash, check collision"]
  e -->|"counter"| g["Base62-encode counter value"]
  c --> h["Store mapping"]
  f --> h
  g --> h
```

## 6. API Design & Protocol Contracts
| Method | Endpoint | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `POST` | `/api/shorten` | Body: { long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at? }. Returns the generated (or validated custom) short code and full short URL. |
| `GET` | `/{shortCode}` | Looks up shortCode, returns an HTTP 301/302 redirect to the original long URL, or 404 if not found or expired. |
| `GET` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}/stats` | Returns click count and basic analytics for a given short URL, if analytics are enabled. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/urls/{shortCode}` | Deletes or deactivates a short URL before its natural expiry, owner-authenticated. |

## 7. Data Models & Storage Schema
### Entity: `urls`
- `short_code (string, primary key, e.g. base62, indexed)`
- `long_url (text, the original destination)`
- `created_at (timestamp)`
- `expires_at (timestamp, nullable)`
- `owner_id (nullable, if user accounts exist)`
*Notes:* The entire hot path only ever needs short_code -> long_url, which is exactly why this fits a key-value store as well as a relational one.

### Entity: `click_events`
- `short_code (string, indexed)`
- `timestamp (timestamp)`
- `referrer (string, nullable)`
- `approx_location (string, nullable, derived from IP)`
*Notes:* Written asynchronously via a queue, never on the synchronous redirect path, so analytics can never slow down a redirect.

## 8. Deep Dives & Edge Case Engineering
### How do you generate the short code itself?
Two real approaches exist. Approach one: hash the long URL (e.g. MD5) and take the first 7 characters, base62-encoded, then check for collisions and re-hash with a salt if one occurs, this is stateless but needs a collision check on every write. Approach two: use a centralized counter (or pre-generated range of counter values handed out to each app server) and base62-encode the counter value itself, guaranteeing uniqueness by construction with zero collision checks, at the cost of needing that counter to be a reliable, available service itself.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Hash-based: no shared state needed between servers, but requires a collision check (an extra database read) on every single write
- Counter-based: zero collision checks ever, but the counter service becomes a new component that must itself be highly available and not become a bottleneck
- A common middle ground: give each app server a pre-allocated range of counter values (e.g. server A gets 1,000,001 to 2,000,000) so most writes never even need to talk to the counter service

### Why cache redirects instead of always hitting the database?
With a 100:1 read:write ratio, the redirect path is where nearly all system load lives, so it's the one path worth optimizing hardest. A cache (Redis or Memcached) holding the hottest short codes in memory turns a database round trip into an in-memory lookup, cutting redirect latency from tens of milliseconds to sub-millisecond, and taking almost all read load off the database entirely.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Cache-aside (read from cache, populate on miss): simple, works well since URL mappings almost never change after creation, so stale cache data is a non-issue
- Skipping the cache entirely would mean every one of the ~500,000 peak reads/sec hits the database directly, which no single database (or even a modest shard count) comfortably survives
- Because a short_code's long_url essentially never changes once created, there's no meaningful cache-invalidation problem here, which is what makes caching this particular system unusually easy compared to most

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- The database is the eventual bottleneck for writes at very high scale; shard by short_code (e.g. hash-based sharding) so writes and the occasional cache-miss read distribute across many machines instead of one.
- A single centralized counter service (if using the counter-based generation approach) can become a bottleneck or single point of failure; solve by handing out pre-allocated ranges to each app server instead of round-tripping to the counter on every write.
- The cache itself needs to be a cluster (not one instance) once traffic is high enough, using consistent hashing to spread hot keys across cache nodes without one node becoming overloaded.
- If analytics volume grows large, the click-event write path needs its own queue and separate storage (e.g. a time-series or analytics-optimized store) so it never competes with the redirect path for resources.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Designing the short code generator around random generation with retry-on-collision without estimating how often collisions actually occur at scale, when they're rare enough that hashing is usually fine, or common enough that a counter-based approach is clearly better.
- ⚠️ ==Forgetting to cache redirects at all== and assuming a single database can handle hundreds of thousands of reads per second directly.
- ⚠️ Writing click analytics synchronously in the same request path as the redirect, adding latency to every single click for a feature that doesn't need to be real-time.
- ⚠️ Choosing a short code length without doing the math on how many codes are actually needed, either wasting characters (URLs longer than necessary) or running out of code space years earlier than expected.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why is a URL shortener a good system to reason about caching with almost no downsides?**

> **Model Answer:** Because a short_code's mapping to a long_url practically never changes once created (there's no 'edit' operation in the core flow), so there's no cache invalidation problem: whatever you cache stays correct indefinitely, which is unusual and makes caching an almost pure win here.

**Q: What happens if two users try to create the same custom alias at the same time?**

> **Model Answer:** This needs a uniqueness constraint enforced at the database level (a unique index on short_code), and the write should be attempted with that constraint, catching the conflict and returning a clear 'alias taken' error to whichever request loses the race, rather than trying to check-then-write in the application layer, which has a race condition window.

# Design a Rate Limiter

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Stripe • Cloudflare • AWS API Gateway` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A rate limiter is a **distributed counting problem** disguised as an algorithm problem: the hard part was never picking token bucket versus sliding window, it's ==keeping one accurate, low-latency count per client== when a hundred stateless app servers are all trying to enforce the same limit at once.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a rate limiter that protects an API from being overwhelmed by any
single client: each API key or user should be allowed at most N requests
per time window, and requests beyond that limit should be rejected quickly
and cheaply, without slowing down the requests that are still allowed
through.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is the limit per API key/user, per IP address, or both, and does it apply globally or per endpoint?
*Why it matters:* Per-IP limiting breaks down behind NAT or shared corporate proxies, and per-endpoint limits (e.g. a cheap read endpoint vs an expensive write endpoint) need separate counters, not one global counter, which changes the key design entirely.

#### Q: Does the limit need to be hard real-time accurate, or is some slack (a client briefly exceeding the limit) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Perfectly exact distributed counting requires synchronous coordination on every request, which adds latency to every allowed request too. Tolerating small slack unlocks much cheaper, eventually-consistent counting schemes.

#### Q: What should happen to a rejected request: a hard 429 error, or should it be queued and retried later?
*Why it matters:* A hard rejection means the limiter only needs to answer 'allow or deny' quickly. A queue-and-retry model turns this into a second system (a request queue with its own backpressure), which is a materially different and larger design.

#### Q: How many distinct clients need independent limits, and how many app servers will be enforcing the limit simultaneously?
*Why it matters:* A handful of clients and one app server could get away with an in-memory counter. Millions of clients across hundreds of app servers is what forces the counter into a shared, external store, which is the entire crux of this design.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Allow a client at most N requests within a rolling or fixed time window (e.g. 100 requests per minute).
- Reject requests over the limit with a clear signal (HTTP 429) and, ideally, a Retry-After header.
- Support different limits for different clients or tiers (e.g. free tier vs paid tier).
- Support independent limits per endpoint, not just one global count per client.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The limiter check itself must add minimal latency, ideally low single-digit milliseconds, since it runs on every single request.**
- **The limiter must work correctly across many app servers enforcing the same limit concurrently, not just on one machine.**
- **The limiter must fail safe under its own infrastructure failure: a rate-limiting outage should not take down the whole API (fail open or fail closed, deliberately chosen, not accidental).**
- **The system must handle at least tens of thousands of rate-limit checks per second at peak without becoming the bottleneck itself.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million active API clients, each with an independent limit
- Average client makes 10 requests/minute, peak clients make up to 1,000 requests/minute
- Every single API request needs a rate-limit check, so check volume equals total request volume
- Total API traffic across all clients averages 50,000 requests/sec at peak

### Calculations & Throughput:

- Sliding window counter (a hybrid that weights the previous and current fixed windows): near sliding-window accuracy at near fixed-window cost, the pragmatic middle ground many production systems actually ship

### Where should the limiter live: client SDK, API gateway, or each individual service?
A client-side SDK can self-throttle to be a good citizen, but it can't be trusted as the actual enforcement point since a malicious or buggy client can simply ignore it. Enforcing at the API gateway means one centralized place checks every request before it reaches any backend service, which is simple to operate and consistent. Enforcing inside each individual service allows different services to have very different limit logic, but means every service reimplements (and can inconsistently implement) the same concern.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Client SDK only: cheap, but not enforceable, exists purely as a courtesy for well-behaved clients, never sufficient alone
- API gateway (centralized): one consistent enforcement point, easy to reason about and change limits globally, but every request pays the cost of a gateway hop and the gateway becomes a component every request depends on
- Per-service enforcement: allows service-specific nuance (e.g. an expensive ML inference endpoint wants a stricter limit than a cheap read endpoint), but risks inconsistent implementations and duplicated counter infrastructure across teams
- The common real-world answer: coarse global limiting at the gateway, plus optional finer per-endpoint limits enforced by individual services for their especially expensive operations

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single Redis instance holding all counters becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure at very high request volume; shard counters across a Redis Cluster by hashing the client key, similar to how a cache would be sharded.
- A synchronous round trip to Redis on every request adds latency and a hard dependency; many production limiters batch or approximate counts locally (e.g. count locally and sync to Redis every N requests or M milliseconds) trading small accuracy loss for much lower latency and Redis load.
- If Redis itself becomes unavailable, the system must have a deliberate fail-open (allow all requests, risking overload) or fail-closed (reject all requests, risking a full outage over a rate-limiter failure) policy, chosen explicitly rather than left to whatever the client library does by default.
- Hot clients (a single very high-volume API key) can still create a hotspot on one Redis key even with sharding; this is usually acceptable since it's bounded to one client's traffic, but extreme cases may need that one client's counter further split and merged.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ ==Storing rate-limit counters in each app server's local memory==, which silently breaks the moment there's more than one app server, since a client can just get routed to a different server with its own fresh counter.
- ⚠️ Picking fixed window without realizing it allows up to **double the intended request rate** right at window boundaries, which matters a lot for strict limits.
- ⚠️ Not deciding what happens when the rate-limit store itself goes down, leaving the system to fail open or closed by accident rather than by design.
- ⚠️ Enforcing rate limits after expensive business logic has already run, instead of as early as possible (ideally at the gateway), wasting compute on requests that were always going to be rejected.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups
**Q: Why does a rate limiter need a shared, external counter store instead of just using each server's local memory?**

> **Model Answer:** Because in any real deployment, a client's requests are load-balanced across many stateless app servers, not pinned to one. If each server kept its own local counter, a client could receive N times the intended limit simply by having requests spread across N servers, since no single server would ever see the client's full request count. A shared store like Redis gives every server the same, consistent view of a client's usage.

**Q: How would you rate-limit fairly when the rate limiter's own Redis backing store is briefly slow or unavailable?**

> **Model Answer:** This requires a deliberate choice: fail open (let requests through when the check can't be performed, protecting availability at the cost of temporarily unenforced limits) or fail closed (reject requests when the check can't be performed, protecting the backend at the cost of availability for legitimate traffic). Most production systems fail open for short blips, since a brief loss of rate limiting is usually less damaging than an outage, but this should be an explicit design decision, documented and tested, not a default nobody chose.

# Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Twitter (Snowflake) • Instagram` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A distributed ID generator exists because uniqueness is easy on one machine and hard across a thousand, so the whole design is about encoding just enough shared context (time and machine identity) into each ID that no two machines ever need to talk to each other to guarantee they **won't collide**.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a service that generates unique IDs for rows/records (like tweets,
orders, or comments) across a large, horizontally sharded system. IDs must
be unique across every shard and server, generated with very low latency,
and ideally roughly sortable by creation time. Design how this ID
generation actually works.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do IDs need to be roughly sortable by creation time, or is pure uniqueness enough?
*Why it matters:* Time-sortable IDs make range queries and pagination ('give me the next page of newest items') trivial with an index. Pure random uniqueness (like a UUID) doesn't sort meaningfully, which pushes sorting work onto a separate index or timestamp column.

#### Q: How many ID-generating machines/services will there be, and how many IDs per second does the system need at peak?
*Why it matters:* This decides how many bits need to be reserved for machine/worker identity versus sequence number within a fixed-size ID (commonly 64 bits total), which is a real budget that has to be planned, not assumed.

#### Q: Can we tolerate a centralized ID service, or does generation need to happen with zero coordination between machines?
*Why it matters:* A single centralized counter service is simple and perfectly ordered but becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure at high write volume. A decentralized scheme (like Snowflake) needs no coordination per ID, at the cost of only approximate time-ordering and needing careful clock handling.

#### Q: What happens if a machine's clock drifts backward (NTP correction, VM migration) mid-operation?
*Why it matters:* Any scheme that embeds a timestamp in the ID can generate a duplicate or out-of-order ID if the clock that generated it moves backward before the next ID is requested. This has to be handled explicitly, not assumed away.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Generate IDs that are unique across every machine and shard in the system, with no coordination required per ID.
- IDs should be roughly sortable by creation time, so a newer ID is numerically larger than an older one.
- Support at least tens of thousands of ID generations per second per machine, with many machines generating concurrently.
- IDs should fit in a standard 64-bit integer for efficient storage and indexing.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **ID generation must be extremely low latency, effectively local, since it happens on the hot path of every single write.**
- **The system must have no single point of failure: losing one machine should not stop any other machine from generating valid, unique IDs.**
- **The scheme must tolerate reasonable clock skew or drift between machines without producing duplicate IDs.**
- **The ID space must be large enough not to exhaust for decades of expected write volume.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 1,000 app server instances, each capable of generating IDs independently
- System needs to support up to 500,000 ID generations per second at global peak
- IDs must remain unique and functional for at least 50 years from launch
- A 64-bit integer ID budget: some bits for time, some for machine identity, some for a per-machine sequence counter

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Per-machine ID rate needed:** 500,000 IDs/sec / 1,000 machines = 500 IDs/sec/machine average, but a single machine must handle bursts well above that, so the sequence-number space per millisecond needs headroom, not just the average
- **Bit budget: timestamp:** 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch gives 2^41 ≈ 2.2 trillion ms ≈ about 69 years of range, comfortably covering the 50-year requirement
- **Bit budget: machine/worker ID:** 10 bits gives 2^10 = 1,024 distinct machine IDs, enough for the 1,000 app servers with a little headroom to grow
- **Bit budget: sequence number:** 12 bits gives 2^12 = 4,096 unique IDs per machine per millisecond, i.e. up to 4,096,000 IDs/sec/machine, far above the 500/sec/machine average and comfortably above realistic bursts

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually drives this design is not the total throughput, which is easily achievable, it's that a single 64-bit integer has to be split into timestamp, machine ID, and sequence bits that all fit together, and once that split is fixed (41/10/12 here), every other property (69-year lifespan, 1,024 machines, 4,096 IDs/ms/machine) falls out of that one decision.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Each app server, on startup, claims a unique small integer worker ID from a
lightweight coordination service (a database row with a uniqueness
constraint, or Zookeeper, touched once per server lifetime, not per
request). From then on, ID generation is entirely local: the server reads
its current millisecond timestamp, combines it with its own worker ID and

### How do you handle a machine's clock moving backward?
If NTP corrects a machine's clock backward, or a VM is paused and resumed, that machine could generate an ID with an earlier timestamp than an ID it already generated moments before, which risks either an ordering violation or, worse, an actual collision if the sequence counter also happens to repeat. **Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- Refuse-and-wait on clock rollback: guarantees no duplicate or out-of-order IDs ever, at the cost of that one machine briefly being unable to generate new IDs during the rollback window (typically milliseconds)
- Ignoring clock rollback entirely: never blocks, but risks actual ID collisions across the same machine's own IDs, which is a correctness bug, not just a minor ordering imperfection

- ⚠️ Not handling clock rollback at all, leaving a real (if rare) path to duplicate or out-of-order IDs in production.
- ⚠️ Under-provisioning the machine-ID bit space for expected fleet growth, forcing a breaking ID-format migration years later when the fleet outgrows it.

# Design a Web Crawler

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Google • Bing • Common Crawl` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A web crawler's real constraint isn't how fast you can download pages, it's that the web is an **adversarial, unbounded graph** with no global coordinator, so the entire design is about disciplined, distributed traversal: ==never hammering one site==, never redoing work you've already done, and never trusting the graph to be finite or well-behaved.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a web crawler that starts from a set of seed URLs, downloads pages,
extracts links from them, and continues crawling those links, eventually
covering a large portion of the reachable web, while being polite to the
sites it crawls and not wasting effort on pages it has already seen or
near-duplicate content. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What's the goal: broad coverage of the whole web, or focused crawling of a specific domain or topic?
*Why it matters:* Broad web-scale crawling needs a URL frontier and dedup system built for billions of pages and effectively unbounded discovery. A focused crawl (e.g. one company's site, or pages matching a topic) is a much smaller, differently-shaped problem that doesn't need the same infrastructure.

#### Q: How aggressively can we crawl any single website, and do we need to respect robots.txt and crawl-delay directives?
*Why it matters:* Politeness constraints (per-domain rate limits, robots.txt) directly shape the URL frontier's design: it can't just be one big queue, it needs to guarantee no domain gets hit too fast, which is a scheduling problem, not just a download problem.

#### Q: Do we need to detect and skip near-duplicate content (not just exact duplicate URLs), like mirrored pages or syndicated articles?
*Why it matters:* Exact-URL dedup is a simple set-membership check. Near-duplicate content detection requires fingerprinting page content (e.g. shingling and similarity hashing), which is a meaningfully harder, separate subsystem.

#### Q: How fresh does crawled content need to be: is this a one-time crawl, or does content need to be periodically re-crawled for changes?
*Why it matters:* A one-time crawl only needs a frontier that shrinks over time. A continuously refreshed index needs a re-crawl scheduling policy (crawl frequently-changing pages more often than static ones), which is an entirely additional layer on top of first-time discovery.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Given a set of seed URLs, crawl them and extract outbound links to discover new URLs.
- Download and store page content for further processing (e.g. indexing).
- Avoid re-crawling the same URL redundantly within a crawl cycle.
- Respect each site's robots.txt rules and avoid overloading any single domain with too many concurrent requests.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **The system must scale horizontally to many crawler workers running concurrently across billions of URLs.**
- **The system must be polite: it must never send an excessive request rate to any single domain, regardless of how large the overall crawl is.**
- **The system must be resilient to individual page failures, malformed HTML, infinite redirect loops, and unreachable hosts, without those failures stalling the rest of the crawl.**
- **Deduplication (seen-URL and near-duplicate content) must keep the crawler from wasting bandwidth and storage reprocessing content it has effectively already seen.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- Target: crawl 5 billion pages within a 30-day cycle
- Average page size (HTML) is roughly 100 KB
- Average site should not be hit more than 1 request per second (politeness)
- Average page has roughly 50 outbound links discovered on extraction

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Required crawl rate:** 5,000,000,000 pages / (30 * 86,400 seconds) ≈ 1,930 pages/sec average, design for several times that at peak to leave room for slow days and retries, so roughly 5,000-10,000 pages/sec sustained
- **Storage for raw page content:** 5,000,000,000 * 100 KB ≈ 500 TB per crawl cycle, requiring distributed blob storage, not a single machine or even a single database
- **URL frontier growth from link discovery:** 5,000,000,000 pages * 50 links/page = 250 billion link references discovered, the large majority of which point to URLs already seen, which is exactly why URL dedup has to be cheap and fast at this volume
- **Politeness-driven worker count:** At 1 request/sec/domain and needing 5,000 pages/sec overall, the frontier must be spreading work across at least 5,000 distinct domains being crawled concurrently at any instant, which is the number that forces the frontier to be domain-aware, not a flat FIFO queue

*Capacity Takeaway:* The single fact that drives this architecture is that politeness limits (roughly 1 request/sec per domain) cap how fast any one site can be crawled, so hitting an aggregate target of thousands of pages/sec is only possible by spreading load across thousands of domains concurrently, which is why the URL frontier has to be a per-domain-aware scheduler, not a simple shared queue.

## 5. High-Level Architecture

# Design a Distributed Cache System (like Redis/Memcached itself)

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Redis Labs • Memcached` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Building the cache itself flips the usual framing: instead of asking how to use a cache, the whole design is about how to spread keys across many memory-bound nodes so any one node's failure or overload doesn't take out the whole cache, which makes **consistent hashing** and replication, not the get/set API, the actual core of the system.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design the cache service itself, not a system that happens to use a cache
in front of a database, but the distributed in-memory key-value store
that other systems would plug in as their cache layer. It needs to store
key-value pairs in memory across many nodes, evict data intelligently
when full, survive individual node failures without losing all cached
data, and let clients find the right node for a given key quickly.
Design it.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Is this a pure look-aside cache (best-effort, losing data is tolerable) or does it need durability guarantees (data must survive a node crash)?
*Why it matters:* A pure best-effort cache can treat node failure as 'those keys are just gone, refetch from the source of truth,' which is much simpler. Requiring durability means adding replication (and the consistency trade-offs that come with it), a materially bigger system.

#### Q: What eviction policy is expected when a node runs out of memory: LRU, LFU, or TTL-based expiry, or some combination?
*Why it matters:* This decides what per-key metadata every node must track (last-access time for LRU, access frequency for LFU, expiry timestamps for TTL) and directly affects memory overhead per entry, which matters a lot at cache scale.

#### Q: How many nodes are expected, and how often do nodes get added or removed (scaling events, failures)?
*Why it matters:* Frequent membership changes make the key-to-node mapping scheme matter enormously: a naive mod-N hashing scheme would remap almost every key on every node change, causing a massive cache-miss storm each time, which is exactly what consistent hashing is designed to prevent.

#### Q: What's the acceptable data-loss window if a node fails: zero (synchronous replication), or a few seconds (asynchronous replication) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* Synchronous replication to a replica before acknowledging a write guarantees no loss but adds latency to every write. Asynchronous replication is faster but accepts a small window where a crash loses the most recent writes, a real trade-off that has to be chosen deliberately, not defaulted into.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- Support basic key-value operations: GET, SET, DELETE, with optional TTL (time-to-live) on a key.

# Design a Notification System

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon SNS • Firebase Cloud Messaging` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> This is a **fan-out plus retry** problem wearing a friendly UI: one internal event has to reliably reach the right user on the right channel, and reliably here means surviving a flaky provider ==without spamming the user twice==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a notification system that can send a message to a user across
multiple channels (push notification, email, SMS), triggered by other
internal services (e.g. "order shipped", "someone liked your post").
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Which channels need to be supported: push, email, SMS, in-app, or all of them?
*Why it matters:* Each channel has a different provider, different latency characteristics, and different failure modes; supporting all four multiplies the integration surface and the retry logic needed.

#### Q: Do users get to choose which channels they receive which notification types on?
*Why it matters:* Per-user, per-notification-type preferences mean a preference lookup has to sit in the pipeline before fan-out, not after, otherwise you send notifications you then have to apologize for.

### How do you prevent a large marketing campaign from starving transactional notifications?
If both a 'your order shipped' notification and a 20-million-user marketing blast go through the exact same queue with the same priority, the marketing blast can flood the queue and delay time-sensitive transactional notifications behind it. The fix is separating them into distinct queues (or priority tiers within one queue system) with independent worker pools, so a campaign's volume can never delay an order confirmation.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**

- Separate queues per priority tier with dedicated worker pools: transactional traffic gets guaranteed capacity regardless of campaign volume, at the cost of more infrastructure to provision and monitor
- A hybrid: one queue with a priority field that workers respect, cheaper to run than fully separate queues, but requires careful worker logic to actually honor priority under load rather than just processing in arrival order

### How do you avoid sending duplicate notifications when a delivery worker retries?
If a worker sends a push notification, then crashes before recording that it succeeded, a retry could resend the exact same notification, annoying the user. The fix is idempotency: each delivery attempt carries a unique idempotency key (derived from notification_id + channel), and either the provider itself supports deduplication by that key, or the worker checks and records delivery status atomically before considering a retry safe to send.

**Trade-offs Evaluated:**
- No idempotency handling: simplest, but a crash-then-retry scenario can double-send, which is a real, visible user-facing bug
- Idempotency keys checked against the provider: relies on provider support (not all providers offer this), but offloads the dedup work
- Idempotency enforced at the delivery-status layer: the worker atomically transitions a delivery from queued to sent before calling the provider, so even a worker crash mid-send leaves a clear, checkable state for a safe retry decision, this is the most robust and provider-independent approach

## 9. Bottlenecks & Horizontal Scaling Solutions
- A single queue and worker pool can't absorb a large campaign burst without delaying transactional traffic; separate queues or priority tiers by traffic class solve this directly.
- Provider rate limits (APNs, email providers, SMS gateways all cap requests per second) become the real ceiling on delivery throughput; workers need their own rate limiting and backoff tuned to each provider's specific limits.
- The preferences lookup, if done as a synchronous database call per notification, can become a bottleneck at high volume; caching preferences (they change rarely) removes this from the hot path.
- As channel count grows (adding in-app, webhook, or third-party integrations), the delivery worker layer needs to stay pluggable, adding a channel should mean adding a new worker type, not modifying the core fan-out logic.

## 10. Common Interview Pitfalls to Avoid
- ⚠️ Routing all notification traffic through one queue regardless of priority, letting a large campaign delay time-sensitive transactional notifications.
- ⚠️ ==Retrying failed deliveries without idempotency protection==, resulting in duplicate notifications reaching the user.
- ⚠️ Checking user preferences after generating and queuing deliveries instead of before, wasting work and risking sending disabled notification types.
- ⚠️ Ignoring provider-specific rate limits and assuming internal system throughput is the only constraint on delivery speed.

## 11. Typical Staff / Senior Interview Follow-ups

> **Model Answer:** A single queue processes roughly in arrival order, so a 20-million-user campaign can bury a time-sensitive 'order shipped' notification behind millions of queued campaign messages, delaying it far beyond what's acceptable. Separate queues with dedicated worker pools guarantee transactional traffic gets processed promptly regardless of how much bulk traffic is in flight.

# Design a Distributed Key-Value Store

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Amazon (DynamoDB) • Riak` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A single-node key-value store is a solved problem, the entire difficulty here is that once you replicate data across machines to survive failure, you're forced to pick, on every single request, some point on the line between **consistency and availability**, and that choice is the whole system.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a distributed key-value store: clients can put(key, value) and
get(key). The store needs to hold far more data than fits on one machine,
keep working when individual nodes fail, and stay available for both
reads and writes even during a network partition. Design the system end
to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do we need strong consistency (every read sees the latest write) or is eventual consistency acceptable?
*Why it matters:* This is the single biggest fork in the design. **Strong consistency** means every write must be acknowledged by a majority before it succeeds, hurting write latency and availability during partitions. **Eventual consistency** allows much higher availability and throughput, at the cost of ==clients occasionally reading stale data==.

#### Q: What's the read:write ratio, and how large are typical values?
*Why it matters:* A read-heavy workload with small values favors aggressive replication and caching; a write-heavy workload with large values (say, blobs) favors a design that minimizes what gets copied across the network on every write.

#### Q: How many node failures should the system tolerate at once, and do we need to survive an entire data center going down?
*Why it matters:* This decides the replication factor (3 is common for single-node-failure tolerance, more for data-center-level tolerance) and whether replicas must be spread across failure domains, not just across machines.

#### Q: Do writes to the same key need to be resolved automatically, or is it acceptable to surface conflicting versions to the application?
*Why it matters:* This decides whether we need vector clocks and app-level conflict resolution (more correct, more complex) or can get away with simple last-write-wins (simpler, but silently drops concurrent writes).

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- put(key, value): store a value under a key, durably.
- get(key): retrieve the most recent value(s) for a key.
- delete(key): remove a key's value.
- The system continues to serve reads and writes even when some nodes are down.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **High availability: the system should accept writes and serve reads even during a node failure or network partition, favoring availability over strict consistency (an AP system).**
- **Horizontal scalability: adding nodes should linearly increase storage capacity and throughput, with no single node holding all the data or seeing all the traffic.**
- **Durability: an acknowledged write must survive the failure of any single node that stored it, via replication.**
- **Low latency: p99 get/put latency should stay in the single-digit milliseconds under normal operation, since this store is meant to be a building block other services call synchronously.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10 billion keys stored, average value size 1 KB
- 50,000 writes/sec and 500,000 reads/sec sustained (10:1 read:write ratio)
- Replication factor of 3 (every value stored on 3 different nodes)
- Each storage node has 4 TB of usable disk

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Raw data size:** 10,000,000,000 keys * 1 KB ≈ 10 TB of unique data
- **Total storage with replication:** 10 TB * replication factor 3 = 30 TB of data actually written to disk across the cluster
- **Minimum node count for storage:** 30 TB / 4 TB per node ≈ 8 nodes minimum just to fit the data, before considering headroom or throughput
- **Write fan-out per put:** 50,000 writes/sec * replication factor 3 = 150,000 physical write operations/sec across the cluster, this is the number that actually drives node count and network capacity, not the 50,000 logical writes/sec

*Capacity Takeaway:* Replication factor multiplies both storage footprint and physical write load, so the real capacity question isn't 'how many logical writes per second' but 'how many physical writes per second does replication factor 3 actually generate', which is why the partitioning and replication strategy has to be decided before anything else.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
Keys are placed on a consistent hash ring: each key hashes to a position
on the ring, and is owned by the next N nodes clockwise from that
position, where N is the replication factor. A client's put(key, value)
is sent (directly, or via a coordinator node) to all N replica nodes for
that key in parallel; the write is considered successful once W of them
acknowledge it. A get(key) similarly queries R replicas in parallel and
returns the most recent version(s), reconciling any conflicts using
version vectors. Consistent hashing means adding or removing a node only
reshuffles a small fraction of keys (the ones near it on the ring),
instead of remapping the entire keyspace the way a simple hash % N scheme
would.

### Interactive Architecture Diagrams

#### Consistent hash ring with replication factor 3

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef client fill:#3b82f6,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef server fill:#6366f1,stroke:#4338ca,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef db fill:#059669,stroke:#047857,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef cache fill:#d97706,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    classDef queue fill:#dc2626,stroke:#b91c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff;
    client["Client"]:::client
    coordinator["Coordinator Node"]:::server
    nodeA[("Node A (replica)")]:::db
    nodeB[("Node B (replica)")]:::db
    nodeC[("Node C (replica)")]:::db
    gossip["Gossip / Membership"]:::server
    client --> coordinator
    coordinator -->|"write, ack"| nodeA
    coordinator -->|"write, ack"| nodeB
    coordinator -->|"write, ack"| nodeC
    coordinator -->|"ring lookup"| gossip
    nodeA -.->|"anti-entropy repair"| nodeB
    nodeB -.->|"anti-entropy repair"| nodeC
```

#### A put(key, value) request, step by step


- Balanced quorum (e.g. W=2, R=2 with N=3, satisfying W+R>N): a common middle ground that tolerates one slow or failed replica on either the read or write path while still guaranteeing overlap, this is the setting most production systems default to

### How do you resolve two writes to the same key that happened concurrently on different replicas?
During a partition, two clients can both write to the same key on different replicas before either write reaches the other, creating two versions with no clear 'later' one. > **Model Answer:** It guarantees that any read quorum and any write quorum must share at least one common replica, so a read is guaranteed to see at least one copy of the most recent successful write. **Q: What happens during a network partition that splits the cluster in two, each half able to reach a write quorum for some keys?**

This is expected and handled by conflict resolution (vector clocks or last-write-wins) once the partition heals and the two sides reconcile, it is the direct cost of choosing availability over strict consistency during the partition.

# Design a Distributed Job Scheduler

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Airbnb (Airflow) • Kubernetes CronJobs` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> Running a job is the easy part, the entire hard part is the handoff: making sure **exactly one worker** picks up exactly one execution of a job at its scheduled time, and correctly noticing and re-assigning it if that worker dies before finishing.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a distributed job scheduler: users define jobs (either one-off,
scheduled for a future time, or recurring on a cron-like schedule), and
the system runs each job exactly once at its scheduled time, across a
fleet of worker machines, even as workers come and go or crash mid-job.
Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: Do jobs need to run exactly once, or is at-least-once (with the job itself being idempotent) acceptable?
*Why it matters:* True exactly-once execution across a distributed system is extremely expensive to guarantee. Most real systems target at-least-once delivery plus idempotent job logic, which is dramatically simpler and is what this design should default to unless told otherwise.

#### Q: How long do jobs typically run, seconds, minutes, or hours, and is there a hard timeout?
*Why it matters:* Short jobs (seconds) make worker-failure detection and re-scheduling cheap and fast. Long-running jobs (hours) need checkpointing or at least a much more patient failure-detection window, or a crashed worker looks indistinguishable from a job that's still legitimately working.

#### Q: Do jobs have priorities or dependencies (job B only runs after job A succeeds)?
*Why it matters:* Dependencies turn this from a flat queue into a DAG scheduler (like Airflow), which needs to track job state and only enqueue a job once its upstream dependencies have completed, a materially more complex system than independent jobs.

#### Q: What's the expected scale: how many distinct scheduled jobs, and how many total executions per day?
*Why it matters:* A system running 10,000 jobs a day can get away with a much simpler single-leader scheduler than one running 100 million executions a day, which needs the scheduling decision itself to be distributed and partitioned.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A user can create a job that runs once at a specific future time, or recurs on a cron-like schedule (e.g. every day at 2am).
- The system assigns each due job execution to exactly one available worker.
- If a worker dies mid-execution, the job is detected as failed and re-assigned to another worker.
- A user can query the status and history of a job's executions (pending, running, succeeded, failed).

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **No job execution should be silently dropped: every due execution either eventually runs or is surfaced as a clear failure, never just disappears.**
- **A single job should not run twice for the same scheduled time under normal operation (at-least-once with idempotent jobs is the accepted fallback, not routine double-execution).**
- **The scheduler must keep working, and jobs must keep getting picked up, even as individual worker nodes fail continuously in a large fleet.**
- **The system must scale to a large worker fleet and a high volume of concurrent job executions without the central scheduling decision becoming a bottleneck.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 5 million distinct scheduled jobs defined in the system
- 50 million job executions triggered per day (many jobs recur multiple times daily)
- Average job runs for 30 seconds; a worker can run 20 jobs concurrently
- Heartbeat interval of 10 seconds, worker considered dead after 3 missed heartbeats (30 seconds)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Execution trigger rate:** 50,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 580 executions/sec average, several times that at peak scheduling windows (e.g. everyone's midnight cron jobs clustering)
- **Concurrent running jobs at peak:** 580 executions/sec * 30 sec average duration ≈ 17,400 jobs running concurrently at steady state, more during peak bursts
- **Worker fleet size needed:** 17,400 concurrent jobs / 20 jobs per worker ≈ 870 workers minimum, plus headroom for peak bursts and failure tolerance, so roughly 1,200-1,500 workers
- **Heartbeat traffic:** 1,500 workers * 1 heartbeat / 10 sec = 150 heartbeats/sec, trivial load, but the 30-second dead-worker detection window is the number that drives how long a crashed job sits unnoticed before re-assignment

*Capacity Takeaway:* The number that actually shapes this architecture isn't total executions per day, it's the peak concurrent-job count combined with the worker-failure detection window, because that pair determines both fleet size and how quickly the system notices and recovers from a dead worker mid-job.

## 5. High-Level Architecture
A scheduling service continuously scans job_definitions, and whenever a
job's next scheduled_time arrives, inserts a pending row into
job_executions (this insert is idempotent, keyed on job_id + scheduled_
time, so a scheduler restart or duplicate scan never creates two rows for
the same due execution). Workers poll a shared, priority-ordered
execution queue and atomically claim ("lease") one pending execution at a
time, flipping it to leased with an expiry timestamp; only one worker can
win that atomic claim. The worker runs the job and heartbeats progress; on
success it marks the execution succeeded. If a worker dies mid-job, it
stops heartbeating, its lease silently expires, and a background reaper
process notices the expired lease and returns the execution to pending so

# Design a Distributed Lock Service

> **Difficulty:** `HARD` | **Target Companies:** `Google (Chubby) • ZooKeeper • etcd` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> A lock is only as trustworthy as the thing storing it, so this system is really about building one small, boring, brutally **strongly-consistent** service that everything else can lean on, and the entire design fight is making sure a crashed or paused lock holder can never block everyone else forever, without accidentally letting ==two holders think they both own the lock at once==.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a lock service that many independent processes across many
machines can use to coordinate: only one process at a time should be able
to hold the lock for a given resource, even though those processes don't
trust each other, can crash at any moment, and can experience arbitrary
network delays. Design the system end to end.

## 2. Clarifying Questions & Key Trade-offs
#### Q: What happens if the process holding the lock crashes or gets network-partitioned from the lock service while still 'holding' it?
*Why it matters:* If locks are held forever until explicitly released, one crashed process permanently deadlocks that resource for everyone. This forces the lock to expire on its own (a lease/TTL), which then forces the harder question of what happens if the original holder wakes back up after its lease already expired.

#### Q: Do clients need to detect if they acted on a lock after their lease had already expired (e.g. wrote to a shared resource after losing ownership)?
*Why it matters:* This is the fencing token problem: a paused process can resume, still believe it holds the lock, and write to the protected resource after another process has already taken over. Without a mechanism to detect and reject that stale write, the lock's guarantee is fake under exactly the failure mode locks exist to prevent.

#### Q: How many distinct locks does the system need to manage concurrently, and how short-lived are typical lock holds?
*Why it matters:* A system managing a few thousand long-held locks (like leader election for a handful of services) is a very different load profile than one managing millions of short-lived per-request locks, and the second case pushes hard on the lock service's own throughput, not just its consistency.

#### Q: Do we need advanced lock types (read/write locks, reentrant locks), or is a simple exclusive mutex enough?
*Why it matters:* A simple exclusive lock is what most coordination use cases (leader election, mutual exclusion on a resource) actually need, and scoping out read/write and reentrant semantics keeps the hard consistency problem from being tangled up with extra lock-semantics complexity.

## 3. Requirements Analysis
### Functional Requirements
- A client can acquire a lock on a named resource; if already held, the client either blocks/waits or is told it's unavailable.
- A client can release a lock it holds.
- A lock automatically expires (via a lease/TTL) if its holder stops renewing it, so a crashed holder can never block the resource forever.
- Every successful lock acquisition returns a monotonically increasing fencing token that downstream systems can use to reject stale writes from a former holder.

### Non-Functional Requirements (SLAs & SLOs)
- **Strong consistency above all else: at any given moment, the lock service must never allow two different clients to both correctly believe they hold the same lock. Availability is secondary to this guarantee.**
- **The lock service itself must be highly available and survive the failure of a minority of its own nodes, since it becomes a single point of failure for every system that depends on it otherwise.**
- **Lock acquire/release/renew operations should be low latency, typically single-digit milliseconds, since they sit on critical coordination paths for other systems.**
- **The service must handle a large number of independent locks and clients without one hot lock or one slow client degrading the service for everyone else.**

## 4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimations
### Assumptions:
- 10,000 distinct active locks at any given time (mostly leader-election and resource-coordination use cases, not per-request locking)
- Each lock holder renews its lease every 2 seconds to keep it alive (well under a 10 second TTL)
- 5,000 acquire/release operations per second across the fleet, on top of renewals
- 5-node consensus cluster (tolerates 2 node failures out of 5)

### Calculations & Throughput:
- **Renewal traffic:** 10,000 active locks / 2 sec renewal interval = 5,000 renewal requests/sec, this is steady background load just to keep locks alive

# Design an Autocomplete / Typeahead Suggestion Service

> **Difficulty:** `MEDIUM` | **Target Companies:** `Google Search • Amazon product search` | **Reading Time:** `20 mins`

> **Core Architectural Principle:**
> The hard constraint here isn't finding matches, a prefix search over millions of strings is a solved data-structure problem, it's returning the **ranked top-K** for that prefix in single-digit milliseconds on every single keystroke, which forces almost all the real ranking work to happen **ahead of time**, not at request time.

## 1. Problem Statement & Scope
Design a typeahead suggestion service: as a user types into a search box,
the system returns the top matching suggestions after every keystroke,
ranked by how likely the user is to actually want them, fast enough that
it feels instant. Design the system end to end.

The precomputation is what turns the request-time cost from O(number of matches * log(matches) for sorting) down to O(prefix length) for the trie walk plus a constant-time read of an already-sorted short list, that's the real unlock, the trie is just the convenient structure that makes precomputing per-prefix lists natural.

**Q: How would you incorporate personalization (a user's own history) without abandoning the precomputed top-K approach entirely?**

> **Model Answer:** Keep the precomputed, globally-ranked top-K list as the base layer, since it's still the fast, cheap majority of the ranking signal, then apply a lightweight, request-time re-ranking pass using a much smaller personalization signal, such as boosting any of the user's own recent searches that happen to match the prefix, or slightly re-weighting the base list using a compact per-user preference vector. This keeps the expensive global ranking work offline while still letting the online path do a small, cheap amount of per-user adjustment rather than computing personalized rankings from scratch on every keystroke.

callout.title: Core Architectural Principle
callout.text: The hard constraint here isn't finding matches, a prefix search over millions of strings is a solved data-structure problem, it's returning the **ranked top-K** for that prefix in single-digit milliseconds on every single keystroke, which forces almost all the real ranking work to happen **ahead of time**, not at request time.
